video.title: Coiling | Spinal Motion | Eye Dominance | Arm Slot - 15 Serves Explained

classification.reason: The coach systematically breaks down serve mechanics (coiling, spinal motion, eye dominance, and arm slot) across multiple pro serves to explain how recreational players should build their own motion.

problem.title_as_question: Why do amateur serves feel awkward, lack velocity, or lose accuracy when copying pro players?
problem.definition: Amateurs often copy aesthetic pro serves (like Federer's) without matching their own individual anatomy, spinal mobility, and ocular dominance, leading to blind aiming, inefficient arm slots, and lost power.
problem.target_player: players copying pro serves or struggling to find effortless power and consistency on serve

symptoms.description: Serve feels awkward and player has poor directional aiming and cannot see opponent cheating
Falling off noticeably to the left during follow-through for a right-handed server
Low serve velocity despite attempting to push hard with the legs

causes.statement: The hitting arm is moving out of the rotational plane of the shoulders, sacrificing leverage and efficiency.
Serve velocity is driven by trunk-loaded internal shoulder rotation, not by forearm pronation or leg push.
Lack of thoracic extension and spinal spring-loading prevents powerful trunk recoil into flexion through contact.
Right-eye dominant (purodextral) players coiling by turning their chest away from the court lose peripheral vision of the target.

angles.summary: Coiling is creating diagonal tension across the trunk by stretching the off shoulder against the hitting-side hip.
Forearm pronation and leg drive are heavily overrated for serve speed compared to trunk and shoulder internal rotation.
Federer can coil by turning his chest away because his left dominant eye preserves peripheral court vision, unlike pure dextral players.
The serve throwing path sends the hand toward the opposite service box while internal shoulder rotation redirects the ball.

solutions.summary: Serve with the head, eyes, and torso facing more forward toward the court if you are right-eye dominant.
Use a purodextral pinpoint stance by stepping the back foot onto the hitting side of the front foot to coil without turning away.
solutions.external_goal: Step back foot onto hitting side of the off foot

solutions.summary: Throw your chest to the sky so trunk rotation twists diagonally upward and forward rather than flat toward the net.
Simplify early prep by directly placing the hitting arm into a 90-90 position to establish rhythm without forced momentum.
Integrate the serve landing with an immediate wide split step and active footwork hops to receive the first ball.
